statement: For a commutative algebra \(K/R\), the order filtration on scalar differential operators has commutative associated graded algebra. The commutator induces a degree-minus-one bracket \(\{\sigma_p(A),\sigma_q(B)\}=\sigma_{p+q-1}([A,B])\). In the smooth real case this identifies with the usual Poisson bracket on fibre-polynomial functions on \(T^*X\), up to the chosen symbol sign convention. The corresponding statement for an arbitrary noncommutative ring is not supplied by these formulas.
fate: \citet[\S7]{vinogradov1972logic} publishes precisely the symbol and Hamiltonian programme for commutative rings. This gives a close mathematical match to the heading once its ambient category is corrected.
present_status: As of November 2026, the commutative symbol bracket is established. It does not provide one unrestricted Hamiltonian calculus on all noncommutative rings.
reconstruction: The associated-graded bracket is the precise published reconstruction of an otherwise terse programme heading.

title: Lemma 1: functoriality in the source and target
notes: With fixed \(N\), \(\operatorname{Diff}_n^+(M,N)\) is contravariant in \(M\); with fixed \(M\), the pointwise module \(\operatorname{Diff}_n(M,N)\) is covariant in \(N\). One displayed composition is typed \(D\circ f:M_1\to M_2\).
statement: For commutative unital \(K/R\), a \(K\)-linear map \(f:M_1\to M_2\) gives \(D\mapsto D\circ f\) from \(\operatorname{Diff}_n^+(M_2,N)\) to \(\operatorname{Diff}_n^+(M_1,N)\). A \(K\)-linear map \(g:N_1\to N_2\) gives \(D\mapsto g\circ D\) on the pointwise operator modules. Both maps preserve order and the stated scalar action.
fate: These elementary functorial properties underpin \citet[\S1]{vinogradov1972logic}. Class A concerns the organized cojet presentation whose proof the November lecture supplies.
present_status: As of November 2026, the functoriality is established. The target in the displayed first composition must be \(N\), a type error rather than a change to the theorem.

title: Lemma 2: first-order operators split into a derivation and multiplication
notes: The notes prove \(A(ab)=aA(b)+bA(a)-abA(1)\) for \(A\in\operatorname{Diff}_1(K,M)\), its converse, and the corollary that \(A-A(1)\) is a derivation.
statement: An \(R\)-linear map \(A:K\to M\) has order at most one exactly when this product formula holds for every \(a,b\in K\). Equivalently, \(A(a)=aA(1)+D(a)\) for a unique \(R\)-derivation \(D\). The subtraction in the corollary means the multiplication map \(a\mapsto aA(1)\), not a constant map.
fate: This is an elementary consequence of the pre-1971 commutator calculus \citep[\S16.8]{grothendieck1967egaiv4}; the derivation functor is part of \citet[\S2]{vinogradov1972logic}. It is expository rather than a new first-order decomposition.
present_status: As of November 2026, the equivalence holds over any commutative unital base, without dividing by 2 and without smoothness. The corrected reading of the subtraction is necessary for additivity.

title: Lemma 3: orders add under composition
notes: For \(A\in\operatorname{Diff}_m(M_1,M_2)\) and \(B\in\operatorname{Diff}_n(M_2,M_3)\), the notes prove \(BA\in\operatorname{Diff}_{m+n}\) by induction and a commutator product rule. Here \(\delta_k\) has the opposite sign from P376.
statement: For commutative \(K/R\), the composition of operators of orders at most \(m,n\) has order at most \(m+n\). With \(\delta_aT=T\circ a-a\circ T\), one has \(\delta_a(BA)=(\delta_aB)A+B(\delta_aA)\). The opposite convention gives the same order condition and the same formal product rule.
fate: The filtered composition law is part of the earlier algebraic operator calculus \citep[\S16.8]{grothendieck1967egaiv4}. The lecture supplies its elementary inductive verification; \citet[\S3]{vinogradov1972logic} uses it to define Spencer differentials.
present_status: As of November 2026, the order bound is established. Equality need not hold: principal symbols can vanish on composition. The local sign switch does not invalidate the argument.

title: Lemma 4: evaluation on cojets is a differential operator
notes: The canonical map \(C:\operatorname{Diff}_n^+(K,N)\to N\), \(C(A)=A(1)\), is called an operator of order \(n\). The proof transfers its iterated commutators to those of \(A\).
statement: With the precomposition \(K\)-module structure on the source, \(C\) has order at most \(n\). Composition with a \(K\)-linear \(f:M\to\operatorname{Diff}_n^+(K,N)\) therefore defines an order-at-most-\(n\) operator \(C\circ f:M\to N\), and this assignment is \(K\)-linear when the resulting operator module uses precomposition.
fate: This evaluation map is the universal cojet operator in \citet[\S1]{vinogradov1972logic}. The proof given on the scan is a correct direct verification, using its chosen commutator sign.
present_status: As of November 2026, the order bound is established. Exact order \(n\) is not asserted: it can drop for particular rings or modules.

title: Lemma 5: currying an operator into a cojet-valued homomorphism
notes: The map sends \(A\) to \(g_A(m)(k)=A(km)\); the notes check order, additivity, and scalar linearity. The first check is called restriction to a submodule.
statement: For \(A\in\operatorname{Diff}_n^+(M,N)\), the map \(k\mapsto A(km)\) has order at most \(n\) because it is the composite of \(A\) with the \(K\)-linear map \(K\to M\), \(k\mapsto km\). The assignment \(m\mapsto g_A(m)\) is \(K\)-linear into the precomposition cojet module, and \(A\mapsto g_A\) is a homomorphism between the indicated operator and Hom modules. The map \(K\to M\) need not be injective.
fate: This is the explicit forward direction of the universal cojet isomorphism published in \citet[\S1]{vinogradov1972logic}. The scan contains the three checks rather than merely announcing the universal property.
present_status: As of November 2026, the construction is established for arbitrary unital modules. The word restriction should be replaced by precomposition with a module map; no torsion-free hypothesis on \(M\) is necessary.

title: Lemma 6: the two cojet maps are mutually inverse
notes: The lecture finishes by computing both composites and concludes \(\operatorname{Diff}_n^+N=\operatorname{Diff}_n^+(K,N)\) as the concrete universal cojet object.
statement: For \(A:M\to N\), evaluation of its curried map gives \(g_A(m)(1)=A(m)\). Conversely, if \(g:M\to\operatorname{Diff}_n^+(K,N)\) is \(K\)-linear, then the curried form of \(C\circ g\) satisfies \((C\circ g)(km)=g(km)(1)=(k\cdot g(m))(1)=g(m)(k)\). Thus the two natural module maps are inverse.
fate: The resulting isomorphism is exactly that stated in \citet[\S1]{vinogradov1972logic}. The November 1971 notebook provides an earlier detailed seminar proof; the paper was received in January 1972.
present_status: As of November 2026, the proof is complete under the commutative-ring and fixed-base conventions already stated. The last equality is a realization of a universal object, not an assertion that the two scalar actions coincide.

title: Infinitesimal homogeneous spaces and infinitesimal torsors
notes: A Lie algebra acts by vector fields; the space is homogeneous when evaluation at every point is onto, and principal when evaluation is an isomorphism. The preceding group definition requires a unique group element carrying one point to another.
statement: Let \(a:\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak X(X)\) be a Lie algebra homomorphism. Transitivity means that \(a_x:\mathfrak g\to T_xX\) is surjective for each \(x\). An infinitesimal torsor has each \(a_x\) invertible and the inverse coframing smooth in the chosen topological category. This definition is infinitesimal: a global integrated action can still have discrete stabilizers.
fate: The principal-space language was already published by \citet[\S3]{gelfandkazhdan1971geometry}, received 5 June 1971. Its precise topological formulation is given in \citet[Definition 2.1]{bernsteinrosenfeld1973homogeneous}. The 15 November lecture explicitly refers to the earlier announcement.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established definition in formal geometry. The terms principal Lie-algebra space and principal group space should not be interchanged without a globalization and stabilizer condition.

title: Finite-dimensional Lie algebras integrate locally, not automatically globally
notes: The underlined answer to when one can pass to a group is: when the Lie algebra is finite-dimensional. No completeness hypothesis is stated.
statement: A smooth action of a finite-dimensional real Lie algebra on a finite-dimensional manifold integrates locally. A global action with these infinitesimal generators requires their completeness; finite-dimensionality by itself is insufficient. Even a complete infinitesimal torsor need not be a free torsor for the simply connected integrating group.
fate: This is a qualification of classical Lie integration, explicitly stated as local integration in \citet[Introduction, pp.~108--109]{bernsteinrosenfeld1973homogeneous}. It is not a new globalization theorem in the notebook.
present_status: As of November 2026, the local reading is correct; the unrestricted global reading is false. No classification of globalizations is inferred from the shorthand.
reconstruction: \ours\ For the global claim, take \(X=(0,1)\) and the action of \(\mathbb R\) generated by \(\partial_x\). Evaluation is an isomorphism everywhere, but its integral curve \(x+t\) leaves \(X\) in finite time. For the freeness issue, translations by \(\mathbb R\) on \(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\) have isomorphic evaluation maps and stabilizer \(\mathbb Z\).

title: Formal vector fields and the origin-fixing formal coordinate group
notes: \(W_n\) consists of formal vector fields. The notes say that its group does not exist because one cannot move; the subalgebra \(L_0\) of fields with zero constant term does integrate and has codimension \(n\). Hamiltonian and volume-preserving variants are mentioned.
statement: For \(n\geq1\), let \(W_n=\operatorname{Der}^{\mathrm{cont}}_{\mathbb R}\mathbb R[[x_1,\ldots,x_n]]\) with its coefficient topology and continuous bracket. The subalgebra \(L_0=\{\sum a_i\partial_i:a_i(0)=0\}\) has vector-space codimension \(n\). The group \(G_n^0\) of invertible formal substitutions fixing the origin is the inverse limit of its finite-jet groups and has Lie algebra \(L_0\) in that category. A general formal series cannot be translated by a nonzero real constant by an unrestricted numerical substitution.
fate: These objects are used in \citet[\S1]{gelfandfuchs1970formal} and \citet[\S3]{gelfandkazhdan1971geometry}; the formal-group and transitive-subalgebra conventions are made explicit in \citet[\S\S4--5]{bernsteinrosenfeld1973homogeneous}. They precede the lecture.
present_status: As of November 2026, the distinction between full formal vector fields and the origin-fixing formal group remains essential. The phrase that no group exists is category dependent; it is not a theorem excluding formal groupoids or every infinite-dimensional integration concept.

title: Automorphisms of the Lie algebra of formal vector fields
notes: The notebook states that the Lie algebra of the automorphism group of \(W_n\) is \(L_0\). It compares this with quotienting an ordinary Lie algebra by its centre.
statement: Over a characteristic-zero field, every continuous Lie algebra automorphism of \(W_n\) is induced by an invertible origin-fixing formal coordinate substitution. Thus, over \(\mathbb R\), the automorphism group with the formal-coordinate, finite-jet group structure has Lie algebra \(L_0\). This is a statement about that topological group, not an unrestricted identification with all algebraic derivations of \(W_n\).
fate: \citet[Theorem 1 and \S3, Theorem 2(1)]{rudakov1969automorphisms} proved preservation of the formal filtration and the coordinate-change description; the paper was received 18 December 1968 and published in Russian in 1969. Theorem 2 also treats the divergence-free, Hamiltonian and contact series. This is prior work, not an unpublished 1971 conjecture.
present_status: As of November 2026, the continuous formal-coordinate classification is established. The notebook comparison with quotient by the centre describes inner automorphisms in the classical case; it does not identify the entire automorphism algebra for arbitrary finite-dimensional Lie algebras.

title: The formal frame bundle as a principal Wn-space
notes: For an arbitrary \(n\)-manifold \(M\), the space \(S(M)\) of jets of local coordinate systems is declared a principal \(W_n\)-space. Equivalence of charts is written as all derivatives of their transition map being zero.
statement: For a smooth \(n\)-manifold \(M\), let \(S(M)\) consist of infinite jets at \(0\) of local diffeomorphisms \((\mathbb R^n,0)\to(M,x)\), for all \(x\). It has a canonical smooth \(W_n\)-valued coframing satisfying the Maurer--Cartan equation, equivalently a principal infinitesimal \(W_n\)-space structure. Two charts define the same jet when their coordinate difference is flat, or their transition has the identity infinite jet. The transition itself cannot have all derivatives zero, since its first derivative is invertible.
fate: \citet[\S3 and \S4, Proposition 1]{gelfandkazhdan1971geometry} announced this construction before the lecture; \citet[Theorem 4.1]{bernsteinrosenfeld1973homogeneous} give a detailed construction and proof in the finite-coordinate category.
present_status: As of November 2026, the formal frame construction is established. The chart-equivalence sentence is a mathematical slip faithfully reproduced by the transcription; correcting it does not require guessing any cancelled words.

title: Other substantive principal Wn-spaces
notes: The final sentence asks whether there are other substantive principal homogeneous spaces, after constructing \(S(M)\). It gives no meaning for substantive or for equivalence of examples.
statement: The identifiable topic is the possible existence or classification of principal infinitesimal \(W_n\)-spaces beyond formal frame spaces. A definite classification problem requires specifying the category, local or global equivalence, permitted quotients and what counts as arising from a manifold. These data are absent, so no unique stronger proposition is reconstructed.
fate: The later theory of \citet[\S\S2, 4--7]{bernsteinrosenfeld1973homogeneous} treats homogeneous spaces and geometric structures systematically. Searches for principal \(W_n\)-spaces and classification did not identify a theorem matching this qualitative question.
present_status: As of November 2026, the particular intended question remains unidentified. This is a limit of the notebook formulation and the checked literature, not evidence that a precise classification problem is open.

title: The characteristic chain map from Lie algebra cochains
notes: A skew multilinear form on \(W_n\) is evaluated on the vectors corresponding to tangent vectors of \(S(M)\). The resulting map is said to commute with the differentials. The printed exponent reads \(s+t-1\).
statement: For a principal infinitesimal \(\mathfrak g\)-space with Maurer--Cartan coframing \(\theta\), a continuous Chevalley--Eilenberg cochain \(c\) gives the differential form \(\Phi(c)(v_1,\ldots,v_q)=c(\theta v_1,\ldots,\theta v_q)\). With matching bracket and Maurer--Cartan signs, \(d\Phi(c)=\Phi(d_{\mathrm{CE}}c)\), giving \(H^*_{\mathrm{cont}}(\mathfrak g)\to H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(S)\). For \(W_n\), continuous scalar cochains depend on finitely many jet coordinates.
fate: This is the cohomological construction in \citet[\S4]{gelfandkazhdan1971geometry}, whose note is explicitly cited on the notebook page. A complete statement and proof are in \citet[\S3, Theorem 3.1]{bernsteinrosenfeld1973homogeneous}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the characteristic map is established. The malformed exponent must be emended together with a consistent left/right convention; its exact intended sign cannot be settled from the two horizontal strokes alone.
reconstruction: Using the convention \(d\theta+\tfrac12[\theta,\theta]=0\) and numbering arguments from 1, the bracket term is \(\sum_{s<t}(-1)^{s+t}c([\xi_s,\xi_t],\xi_1,\ldots,\widehat\xi_s,\ldots,\widehat\xi_t,\ldots,\xi_{q+1})\). Opposite action conventions change the displayed sign consistently. No literal equality sign belongs in this exponent.

title: Bernstein’s finite-coordinate differential calculus on jet towers
notes: After the heading I. Bernstein, an infinite-dimensional manifold is defined as an inverse limit of finite-dimensional manifolds with onto maps; functions are the union of the finite-stage function rings. The de Rham differential is then written by its vector-field formula.
statement: For the jet towers in question one may use inverse systems whose sufficiently high stages are compatible affine bundles over a fixed finite stage. Their inverse limits admit charts modelled on \(\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\). Scalar functions and forms are locally pulled back from a finite stage; vector fields and the exterior differential are defined compatibly. The local finite-stage condition is more general than requiring a single global stage for every smooth function. Arbitrary surjective inverse systems alone do not guarantee this manifold structure.
fate: Bernstein’s intervention is developed with Rosenfeld in \citet[\S1, Definitions 1.1--1.10, Proposition 1.1 and Example 1.1]{bernsteinrosenfeld1973homogeneous}, received 29 March 1973 and published in 1973. That paper explicitly distinguishes its smooth finite-coordinate category from an arbitrary inverse limit.
present_status: As of November 2026, the construction is established for the formal jet spaces used here. The omitted local and bundle hypotheses are material; the statement should not be exported as a definition of all infinite-dimensional smooth manifolds.
speaker: I. N. Bernstein (intervention)

title: The formal Lie algebra is an inverse limit as a vector space
notes: The Lie algebra is described parenthetically as a projective limit of finite-dimensional ones with the corresponding topology. Taken literally as finite-dimensional Lie algebra quotients, this excludes the main example.
statement: In the formal-vector-field setting the underlying topological vector space is an inverse limit of finite-dimensional jet spaces, and the Lie bracket is continuous. The finite coefficient truncations of \(W_n\) are not Lie algebra quotients: order filtrations are not ideals because a constant vector field lowers vanishing order. No projective system of these truncated Lie algebras is required.
fate: \citet[\S0.1]{gelfandfuchs1970formal} use the topological vector-space formulation, and \citet[\S2, preceding Definition 2.1]{bernsteinrosenfeld1973homogeneous} specify that \(\mathfrak g\) is modelled on \(\mathbb R^k\) or \(\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\) as a vector space.
present_status: As of November 2026, the continuous Lie algebra formulation is standard. The literal finite-dimensional Lie-quotient reading is an error; finite jet vector spaces suffice for the subsequent continuous-cochain construction.
reconstruction: \ours\ In one variable, \([\partial_x,x^{k+1}\partial_x]=(k+1)x^k\partial_x\). Thus the fields vanishing to order at least \(k+1\) are not stable under bracketing with all of \(W_1\), and the proposed quotient bracket is not well defined.
speaker: I. N. Bernstein (intervention)

title: Relative cochains and descent of basic forms
notes: The relative complex consists of cochains \(c\) for which both \(c\) and \(dc\) vanish when an argument lies in \(\mathfrak p\). A form on the base is obtained by lifting tangent vectors; independence of the point in the fibre is asserted.
statement: The relative complex is \(C^*(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak p)=\{c:i_Xc=i_Xdc=0\text{ for every }X\in\mathfrak p\}\), equivalently horizontal and \(\mathfrak p\)-invariant cochains. For a compatible bundle \(P\to X\) of principal infinitesimal spaces whose fibres are connected principal \(\mathfrak p\)-spaces, the characteristic forms descend and give \(C^*(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak p)\to\Omega^*(X)\). With a disconnected structure group \(H\), one must require invariance under all of \(H\), as well as horizontality for its Lie algebra.
fate: The relative-complex definition is classical. The homogeneous-space descent in the intervention is formulated precisely by \citet[\S3, Proposition 3.2, Theorem 3.2 and Remark 3.2]{bernsteinrosenfeld1973homogeneous}; Proposition 3.2 explicitly assumes connected fibres.
present_status: As of November 2026, the construction is established with those hypotheses. Horizontality gives independence of lifts, while infinitesimal invariance gives independence only within a connected fibre component; these are different steps.
speaker: I. N. Bernstein (intervention)

title: Relative Lie algebra cohomology need not equal the cohomology of a homogeneous space
notes: The line after the relative-complex definition identifies its cohomology with that of the quotient in the classical case, without compactness or other comparison hypotheses.
statement: For a Lie group \(G\) and closed subgroup \(H\), relative cochains describe suitable \(G\)-invariant differential forms on \(G/H\), including invariance under disconnected isotropy components when necessary. Their inclusion in all differential forms is not generally a quasi-isomorphism. The characteristic construction gives a homomorphism on cohomology; equality requires an additional comparison theorem.
fate: \citet[Theorem 3.2 and Remark 3.2]{bernsteinrosenfeld1973homogeneous} assert the homomorphism, not a general isomorphism. The notebook’s unrestricted equality is therefore not part of the verified published result.
present_status: As of November 2026, the unrestricted equality is false, already in dimension one. This is an elementary correction, not an unresolved comparison problem.
reconstruction: \ours\ Let \(G=(\mathbb R,+)\) and \(H=\{0\}\). The abelian one-dimensional Lie algebra has \(H^1(\mathfrak g;\mathbb R)=\mathbb R\), represented by its nonzero linear functional. Its corresponding invariant form on \(G\) is \(dx\), but \(dx=d(x)\), so \(H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb R)=0\).
speaker: I. N. Bernstein (intervention)

title: Removing linear frames leaves a space homotopy equivalent to the manifold
notes: \(S(M)\) is said to be homotopy equivalent to the first-frame bundle, while \(S(M)/GL(n,\mathbb R)\) is homotopy equivalent to \(M\). A marginal line mentions a map \(M\to S(M)\); later, choices are associated with a connection.
statement: The projection from formal frames to first frames has contractible higher-jet fibres. Similarly, the bundle \(S(M)/GL(n,\mathbb R)\to M\) has contractible fibre, and is a homotopy equivalence for a smooth paracompact manifold. A connection provides a formal exponential section of this quotient. A section of the full frame space would also choose a frame of \(TM\) and generally does not exist.
fate: The formal-coordinate construction is in \citet[\S3]{gelfandkazhdan1971geometry}. The contractible higher-jet-fibre argument is made explicit in \citet[\S8, Theorems 8.3--8.4]{bernsteinrosenfeld1973homogeneous}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the two homotopy statements are established. The unclear marginal word is left unresolved; if the marginal map means a section, its target must be the quotient unless a global framing has been assumed.
speaker: I. N. Bernstein (intervention)

title: The truncated characteristic polynomial ring in relative Wn-cohomology
notes: The relative cohomology is described by generators \(\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_n\), written as having degree \(2n\), with products of degree greater than \(2n\) zero. The later page cites Gelfand and Fuks, Izvestiya, 1971.
statement: With real coefficients and continuous cochains, the group-relative characteristic complex gives \[H^*(W_n,GL(n,\mathbb R))\simeq\mathbb R[c_1,\ldots,c_n]/I_{>2n},\qquad |c_i|=2i.\] Here \(I_{>2n}\) is the ideal generated by monomials of cohomological degree greater than \(2n\). Group-relative means horizontality for \(\mathfrak{gl}_n\) and invariance under the full linear group. The polynomial generators have different degrees; the quotient is essential.
fate: The underlying formal-vector-field computation was published by \citet{gelfandfuchs1970formal}, received 4 November 1969 and published in Russian in 1970. Its English printing carries 1971 copyright, explaining the notebook date. The exact relative statement is \citet[Theorem 10.2]{bernsteinrosenfeld1973homogeneous}; see also \citet[\S2, pp.~125--126]{bott1976characteristic}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the truncated relative ring is established. It is not the untruncated cohomology of \(BGL_n\), and replacing every generator degree by \(2n\) loses the result.
speaker: I. N. Bernstein (intervention)

title: Chern–Weil classes from formal frames and the role of a connection
notes: The images of the generators are linked to Chern classes of the tangent bundle and to Pontryagin classes. Forms are canonical upstairs; nonuniqueness appears when a connection is chosen to obtain forms on \(M\).
statement: Normalize the formal curvature generators so that their characteristic images are \(c_i(TM\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C)\) in real cohomology. Odd Chern classes of a complexified real bundle vanish over \(\mathbb R\), and \(p_i(TM)=(-1)^i c_{2i}(TM\otimes\mathbb C)\) in the standard convention. Pulling a fixed universal cocycle back along a formal exponential section gives a differential-form representative; changing the connection changes the representative by an exact form, not its cohomology class.
fate: This is the classical Chern--Weil construction expressed through \citet{gelfandkazhdan1971geometry}. The normal-bundle version is identified in \citet[Theorem 10.5]{bernsteinrosenfeld1973homogeneous}, whose normalization sends its generator \(c_{2i}\) directly to \(p_i\). \citet[\S4]{bott1976characteristic} verifies the corresponding characteristic map.
present_status: As of November 2026, the characteristic classes are established and independent of the auxiliary connection. The notebook’s Chern/Pontryagin wording should be read with complexification and normalization stated, not as two unrelated sets of real tangent-bundle classes.
speaker: I. N. Bernstein (intervention)

title: Formal transverse frames of a foliation
notes: For a codimension-\(n\) foliation, transverse formal coordinates define \(S_{\mathcal F}(M)\); the notes stress that this is not itself supplied with the claimed natural principal Lie-algebra action. Adapted full coordinates define \(S^{\prime}_{\mathcal F}(M)\), a principal \(W_{N,n}\)-space, with a leaf-tangent subalgebra \(L\) and quotient \(W_n\).
statement: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a regular smooth foliation of codimension \(n\) on an \(N\)-manifold. In formal coordinates \((y,z)\), with \(y\in\mathbb R^n\) transverse, \(W_{N,n}\) consists of fields whose \(y\)-components depend only on \(y\). The ideal \(L\) of fields tangent to the standard leaves has quotient \(W_{N,n}/L\simeq W_n\). Adapted formal frames give a homogeneous pair with isotropy \(L\), hence \(C^*(W_n)=C^*(W_{N,n},L)\to\Omega^*(S_{\mathcal F}(M))\). Passing to full linear-group basic cochains yields the normal-bundle characteristic map on \(M\), since \(S_{\mathcal F}(M)/GL_n\to M\) has contractible higher-jet fibres.
fate: The characteristic-class programme was announced by Bernstein and Rosenfeld in 1972, as recorded in reference [3] and the introduction of their detailed \citet[\S\S6, 8--10]{bernsteinrosenfeld1973homogeneous}. That full paper, received 29 March 1973, verifies the homogeneous-space and characteristic-map mechanism. The present notebook records Bernstein’s 1971 intervention.
present_status: As of November 2026, this construction is established for regular smooth foliations. The transverse quotient and the adapted full-frame principal space have different roles; merely postulating a \(W_n\)-action on the former would omit the actual descent argument.
speaker: I. N. Bernstein (intervention)

title: Bott vanishing for the real normal bundle
notes: The explicit formula kills products of the \(\psi_i\) of degree \(>2n\). The following sentence appears to change this to \(\geq2n\), although the additional stroke is uncertain; the result is named Bott’s theorem.
statement:
For a regular \(C^\infty\) foliation of real codimension \(n\) with normal bundle \(
u=TM/T\mathcal F\), every monomial in the real Pontryagin classes of \(
u\) having total cohomological degree strictly greater than \(2n\) vanishes. Equivalently, the corresponding real Chern classes of \(
u\otimes\mathbb C\) satisfy the truncated polynomial relations. This gives no blanket vanishing in degree exactly \(2n\), and does not assert vanishing of integral torsion classes.
fate: This is the prior obstruction of \citet{bott1970integrability}, from the Berkeley symposium of July 1968, printed in 1970. The formal-cohomology deduction is explicit in \citet[Theorem 10.2, Theorem 10.5 and Corollary 10.1]{bernsteinrosenfeld1973homogeneous} and is revisited by \citet[\S4]{bott1976characteristic}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the strict-degree real-cohomology theorem is established. The scan does not justify silently adopting the stronger boundary inequality; the preceding clear formula supplies the mathematically correct bound.
speaker: I. N. Bernstein (intervention)

title: Characteristic obstruction to homotoping a distribution to a foliation
notes: The last sentence before Arnold’s new heading calls the vanishing relation an obstruction to being homotopically integrable.
statement: Given a smooth codimension-\(n\) subbundle \(D\subset TM\), ask whether it is homotopic through subbundles of the same rank to the tangent distribution of a regular foliation. A necessary condition is that every real Pontryagin monomial of \(TM/D\) of degree \(>2n\) vanish. The statement is an obstruction, not a sufficient criterion.
fate: This is the same integrability problem and Bott obstruction already indexed as GP-1970-26, occurrences 1970-206.1 and 1970-206.2. The notebook supplies a new formal-cohomology derivation of the known obstruction \citep{bott1970integrability}; its characteristic interpretation is verified in \citet[\S4]{bott1976characteristic}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the necessary condition is established and recurs here. No claim of a complete classification of integrable homotopy classes is made on the basis of the literature checked for this occurrence.
reconstruction: \ours\ A homotopy \(D_t\) defines a vector bundle over \(M\times[0,1]\); its quotient bundles at the endpoints are isomorphic. Their Pontryagin classes therefore agree. If \(D_1\) is integrable, Bott vanishing for \(TM/D_1\) gives the stated necessary condition for \(TM/D_0\).
speaker: I. N. Bernstein (intervention)

title: Geometric meaning and arithmetic of an unnamed foliation invariant
notes: Arnold writes \(dw/dz=P(z,w)/Q(z,w)\), describes a foliation on \(\mathbb{CP}^{2}\) away from several points, and mentions an invariant on a three-dimensional complex manifold described as ``point--vector''. He asks for its geometric characterization and integrality or rationality.
statement: The equation, after homogenization and removal of its singular locus, determines a holomorphic line distribution on an open subset of \(\mathbb{CP}^{2}\). The notes do not specify the auxiliary threefold, the characteristic cocycle, its degree, a cycle on which to evaluate it, or its normalization. Consequently no definite integrality or rationality assertion can be extracted.
reconstruction: The interpretation as a holomorphic line distribution is standard reconstruction. Identifying the threefold with a particular frame bundle, or the invariant with a Bott or Godbillon--Vey class, would add information absent from the notebook.
fate: Targeted searches combining Arnold, the 1971 date, foliation invariants, rotation numbers, projective plane, and rationality did not identify an exact publication. The thematic proximity to characteristic classes does not establish a match.
present_status: As of November 2026: unidentified from the surviving statement. This is not evidence that a well-defined problem remains open; recovering the actual cocycle is prerequisite to further work.

title: Recovering rotation numbers from the proposed invariant
notes: The final exercise asks to define rotation numbers as invariants of the same kind, and the preceding sentence calls the construction a generalization of Poincar\'e rotation numbers.
statement: For comparison, an orientation-preserving circle homeomorphism \(f\), with lift \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(F(x+1)=F(x)+1\), has rotation number \(\rho(f)=\lim_{n\to\infty}(F^n(x)-x)/n\pmod{\mathbb Z}\). The requested realization of this number by the unnamed foliation invariant is not specified well enough to formulate an equivalence.
reconstruction: The displayed modern definition is supplied solely to distinguish the classical invariant from the unidentified proposed realization. It is not claimed to be the notebook's missing construction.
fate: The classical rotation number predates the seminar, but a publication matching the proposed characteristic-class realization was not identified by the searches recorded in the research log. No cross-year problem identifier was reused merely because earlier foliation items mention \(\mathbb{CP}^{2}\).
present_status: As of November 2026: the exercise's intended map from the auxiliary geometry to \(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\) remains unidentifiable in these notes.

title: Quadratic polynomials, involutions, and twisted duals
notes: The talk begins with \(q(x)=\sum a_{ij}x_ix_j\) over a commutative ring, and says that when \(2\) is invertible one may use symmetric matrices uniquely. Over a ring with involution it uses \(f(u\mu,v\lambda)=\mu^*f(u,v)\lambda\), and corrects the left/right module description of \(V^*=\operatorname{Hom}_A(V,A)\).
statement: For an associative unital ring \(A\) with anti-involution \(*\), give \(V^*\) the right action \((f\cdot a)(v)=a^*f(v)\). Then right-linear maps \(L:V\to V^*\) correspond to sesquilinear pairings \(b(u,v)=L(u)(v)\). Over a commutative ring with \(2\in A^\times\), formal homogeneous quadratic polynomials on \(A^n\) have unique symmetric coefficient matrices; arbitrary polynomial functions over a finite ring need not determine their polynomial expressions.
reconstruction: The twisted right action makes the notebook's successive corrections coherent. The qualification ``formal polynomial'' avoids an unnecessary assertion about polynomial functions.
fate: These are the algebraic conventions underlying the form-ring theory, already used before the talk in Vaserstein's 1970 paper. A precise modern statement appears in \citet[\S1]{bakvavilov2000structure}.
present_status: As of November 2026: standard definitions. The crossed-out module adjectives are not evidence for a different duality convention.

title: The form parameter and quadratic forms as a quotient
notes: A central \(\varepsilon\) satisfies \(\varepsilon\varepsilon^*=1\), and an additive subgroup \(\Lambda\) lies between \(\{x-\varepsilon x^*\}\) and \(\{x=-\varepsilon x^*\}\), with \(a^*\Lambda a\subseteq\Lambda\). Quadratic forms are sesquilinear forms modulo the subgroup defined by \(X=-\varepsilon X^*\) and \(X(v,v)\in\Lambda\).
statement: Fix \((A,*,\varepsilon,\Lambda)\) with precisely those conditions. On a right \(A\)-module \(V\), identify sesquilinear forms \(Q,Q'\) when \(X=Q-Q'\) satisfies \(X(u,v)+\varepsilon X(v,u)^*=0\) and \(X(v,v)\in\Lambda\) for all \(u,v\). This quotient retains both the associated \(\varepsilon\)-hermitian pairing and the diagonal refinement modulo \(\Lambda\).
reconstruction: The matrix star is interpreted as conjugate transpose; otherwise the displayed quotient has no invariant meaning.
fate: The framework is that of Bak's form rings, whose pre-1972 origin is documented in \citet[introduction and \S1]{bakvavilov2000structure}. The latter gives the exact bounds on \(\Lambda\), the conjugation condition, and the corresponding quadratic module.
present_status: As of November 2026: established form-ring language, particularly essential when \(2\) is not invertible.

title: Hermitianization and the failure of the diagonal alone at maximal parameter
notes: The notes define \((u,v)_q=Q(u,v)+\varepsilon Q(v,u)^*\) and \(|u|_q=Q(u,u)+\Lambda\). The final line says that for maximal \(\Lambda\) the quadratic form can be recovered from its \(|u|_q\), with ``linearization'' in parentheses.
statement: Both \(b_q\) and \(q_\Lambda\) are independent of the representative. At \(\Lambda=\Lambda_{\max}\), the quotient quadratic form is determined by \(b_q\), not generally by \(q_\Lambda\). For a field with trivial involution, \(\varepsilon=-1\), and \(\Lambda=A\), every diagonal refinement takes values in \(A/\Lambda=0\), while nonzero alternating pairings exist.
reconstruction: The replacement of the diagonal expression by the hermitianized pairing is a mathematical emendation. The counterexample diagnoses the literal assertion without attributing it to the speaker's intended formulation.
fate: The two pieces of data and their relation are explicit in \citet[\S1, especially Lemma 1.1]{bakvavilov2000structure}. The scan confirms the diagonal symbol in the disputed sentence; it is not an English translation error.
present_status: As of November 2026: the corrected statement is standard; the displayed maximal-parameter assertion is false literally.

title: Hyperbolic quadratic modules and nonsingularity
notes: The example is called Hamiltonian or hyperbolic: \(H(U)=U\oplus U^*\), with a representative \(Q(u+f,u'+f')=f(u')\). A triangular matrix and the alternating matrix \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) are displayed. Nonsingularity means that the induced map to the dual is an isomorphism.
statement: For finite projective \(U\), the evaluation pairing defines a hyperbolic \(\Lambda\)-quadratic module on \(U\oplus U^*\). With the compatible ordering of summands, its hermitianized matrix is \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&I\\\varepsilon I&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), up to exchanging the two blocks. The alternating matrix in the notes is the specialization \(\varepsilon=-1\).
reconstruction: Finite projectivity supplies the canonical bidual isomorphism and hence nonsingularity. The sign is restored as a parameter rather than silently fixing the entire talk to the symplectic case.
fate: See \citet[\S1, hyperbolic quadratic module]{bakvavilov2000structure}; Vaserstein's own earlier treatment of stable unitary and orthogonal groups is \citet{vaserstein1970stabilization}.
present_status: As of November 2026: standard hyperbolic construction; the displayed minus sign cannot represent all the form parameters introduced on P000396.

title: Grothendieck--Witt group versus Witt quotient
notes: Nonsingular forms on finite projective modules form a semigroup under orthogonal sum. Its group completion is first called the Witt group, then explicitly corrected to Witt--Grothendieck; the Witt group is the quotient by Hamiltonian forms. The notation is \(K_0O(A)\), with the form parameters suppressed.
statement: The group completion of isometry classes of nonsingular \(\Lambda\)-quadratic forms is \(GW_0(A,*,\varepsilon,\Lambda)\). Its quotient by the subgroup generated by hyperbolic forms is the corresponding Witt group. Witt cancellation, in its familiar form, holds for finite-dimensional nonsingular quadratic spaces over a field of characteristic different from two; analogous involutive versions require their own hypotheses.
reconstruction: The notebook's correction is retained. The characteristic restriction is supplied for the classical cancellation statement, without asserting an unrestricted theorem for every parameter over every division ring.
fate: These are classical distinctions in the theory of forms, rather than a new higher \(K\)-theory result. The stable group framework had already appeared in \citet{vaserstein1970stabilization}; \citet[\S1]{bakvavilov2000structure} fixes the parameter conventions used here.
present_status: As of November 2026: established. Conflating group completion with the hyperbolic quotient would change subsequent examples.

title: Hyperbolic complements and the finiteness restriction
notes: Theorem 1 says that every finite projective module with a quadratic form is an orthogonal summand of \(H(A^n)\). A following remark says that allowing cancellation by arbitrary modules makes the group zero, illustrated by \(a+b+a+b+\cdots\).
statement: For a nonsingular quadratic module \((P,q)\), the diagonal in \((P,q)\perp(P,-q)\) is a lagrangian, giving a hyperbolic module; choosing \(P\oplus P'\cong A^n\) supplies a finite hyperbolic complement. If the category instead admits countable orthogonal sums, the isomorphism \(X\oplus\bigoplus_{m\ge1}X\cong\bigoplus_{m\ge1}X\) forces \([X]=0\) in its group completion.
reconstruction: Nonsingularity is inherited from the immediately preceding definition and is indispensable: a singular form cannot be a nonsingular orthogonal summand of a nonsingular form. The infinite-sum remark is an Eilenberg swindle, not a statement that ordinary finite-projective Witt groups vanish.
fate: Both arguments belong to the standard stable algebraic framework; compare the finite-projective definitions in \citet[\S12]{bass1964stable}. No new general vanishing theorem is being announced.
present_status: As of November 2026: valid with the stated category restrictions. The finite-projective and arbitrary-module group completions must remain distinct.

title: Field and integral examples: stable invariants are not complete isometry invariants
notes: Examples over a field with \(\varepsilon=\pm1\) are followed by \(K_0O(A)=\mathbb Z\). Over \(\mathbb Z\), the notes discuss dimension and signature, and for \(\varepsilon=-1\) distinguish \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z\) from \(2\mathbb Z\), mentioning the Arf invariant.
statement: Nonsingular alternating forms over a field are classified by their even dimension, yielding \(GW_0^{\mathrm{alt}}\cong\mathbb Z\). The corresponding blanket statement for symmetric forms is false: over \(\mathbb R\), positive and negative indices give \(GW_0(\mathbb R)\cong\mathbb Z^2\). Integral rank and signature do not classify definite even unimodular lattices up to isometry. For a unimodular alternating integral pairing, a quadratic refinement modulo two induces a nonsingular quadratic space on the reduction modulo two, whose Arf invariant distinguishes its two symplectic equivalence classes in positive even dimension.
reconstruction: The examples are separated by parameter and equivalence relation. The Arf statement is about the induced mod-two refinement, not an invariant of the underlying alternating bilinear pairing alone.
fate: The form-parameter distinction is explicit in \citet[\S1]{bakvavilov2000structure}. The general framework predates the talk. The Arf discussion is thematically related to earlier occurrence 1970-228.2, but the notebook poses no recurrent question requiring a problem-index identification.
present_status: As of November 2026: the corrected examples are standard; the universal \(\mathbb Z\) claim and an unrestricted isometry classification by rank and signature are false.

title: An unspecified K-group of a finite group ring
notes: The notes say that little is known for \(A=\mathbb Z[g]\), and give \(g=\mathbb Z_p\times\mathbb Z_q\) as an example where \(K_0\) is unknown.
statement: A precise computation would require specifying whether \(K_0\) means ordinary projective \(K_0\), its reduced class group, or the hermitian group \(K_0O\) of this talk; in the last case one must also fix the group-ring involution, \(\varepsilon\), and \(\Lambda\). The roles and assumptions on \(p,q\) are not supplied.
reconstruction: No particular group-ring conjecture is substituted for these omitted choices. In particular, a theorem about projective ideal class groups would not automatically settle the hermitian question.
fate: Searches of Vaserstein's publications and the surrounding algebraic \(K\)-theory literature did not identify a unique computation with these parameters. The supplied prior index contains no exact recurrence.
present_status: As of November 2026: the historical ``unknown'' cannot be converted into a present-day open-problem claim without identifying the functor.

title: The mass-formula lower bound for rank-32 even unimodular lattices
notes: A numerical aside mentions approximately \(80\cdot10^6\) forms in 32 variables with determinant one.
statement: Let \(\Omega_{32}\) be the integral isometry classes of positive-definite even unimodular lattices of rank 32. The classical mass \(m_{32}=\sum_{L\in\Omega_{32}}|\operatorname{Aut}L|^{-1}\) satisfies \(|\Omega_{32}|\ge\lceil2m_{32}\rceil=80,618,466\), since every such lattice has the two automorphisms \(\pm1\). This is a lower bound, not an exact count.
reconstruction: Positive definiteness, evenness, integral isometry, and the lower-bound interpretation are restored from the mass formula. The notebook gives only the rounded number and determinant-one condition, so the identification is strong but not textually complete. An independent exact-arithmetic check of the mass normalization and the counting inequality is given in the editorial verification \ref{verification:mass}; this checks the historical numerical identification and is not a new lattice-classification result.
fate: The number is the classical Minkowski--Siegel mass bound. An exact retrospective check is \citet[\S6, comparison following Corollary 17]{king2003mass}, which prints 80,618,466 and obtains the stronger lower bound 1,162,109,024. Its preprint first appeared in 2000 and the paper in 2003; that later improvement is not attributed to the 1972 speaker.
present_status: As of November 2026: the recovered lower bound is established and has long been surpassed. No assertion of a complete modern enumeration is made.

title: Matrix-ring invariance and the choice of duality
notes: The notes record equality of the \(K\)-groups of \(A\) and of its matrix rings.
statement: For a unital associative ring and \(r\ge1\), Morita equivalence yields \(K_n(M_r(A))\cong K_n(A)\) for ordinary algebraic \(K\)-theory. In a hermitian version the equivalence must transport the involution, duality, and form parameter; an arbitrary unrelated involution on the matrix ring is not covered.
reconstruction: Ordinary Morita invariance is the secure statement. The duality requirement prevents importing it unchanged into every hermitian theory mentioned in the talk.
fate: The low-degree stable-algebra form is already in \citet[\S\S12--14]{bass1964stable}; the higher-theory comparison is subsequently incorporated into \citet{vaserstein1973foundations}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established, with the stated compatibility qualification for forms.

title: Stable orthogonal groups and hermitian K1
notes: The stable group \(O(A)\) is formed from automorphism groups of \(H(A^n)\); \(K_1O(A)\) is its abelianization, with an elementary subgroup playing the role of commutators.
statement: Fix the form ring and use stabilization by a hyperbolic plane. The stable unitary group \(U(A,\Lambda)\) has the stable elementary subgroup \(EU(A,\Lambda)\); under the standard stable form-ring conventions their quotient is hermitian \(K_1\). Assertions about a single finite-rank group require separate stability bounds and cannot be read off from this direct limit.
reconstruction: The letter \(O\) is understood in the notebook's broad parameter-dependent sense, including symplectic and unitary specializations, rather than only the usual orthogonal group of a field.
fate: This is the subject of \citet[\S1, Theorems 1.4 and 1.4O]{vaserstein1970stabilization}, received 29 January 1969 and published in the Russian original in 1970 (English translation copyright 1971). It therefore predates the talk. The general form-parameter convention is made explicit in \citet[\S\S1--2]{bakvavilov2000structure}.
present_status: As of November 2026: standard stable hermitian \(K_1\); no unstated finite-rank stability theorem is attributed to the lecture.

title: Perfect groups, universal central extensions, and second homology
notes: The middle of P000399 records \(H_2(G,\mathbb Z)\to\widetilde G\to G\) with the condition \([G,G]=G\), following a Steinberg-type extension for the elementary classical group.
statement: A group \(G\) admits a universal central extension if and only if it is perfect. Its kernel is naturally \(H_2(G;\mathbb Z)\). For the stable elementary linear group of an associative unital ring \(A\), the Steinberg group \(\operatorname{St}(A)\to E(A)\) is its universal central extension, with central kernel \(K_2(A)\cong H_2(E(A);\mathbb Z)\).
reconstruction: The general perfect-group theorem is read separately from the proposed hermitian model. The verified stable linear case is a comparator; it does not by itself prove the same presentation theorem for every form parameter or every finite-rank classical group.
fate: The relation with perfect groups and the classical Steinberg--Milnor construction predates the lecture. \citet[historical introduction, p.95; \S6, Theorem 6.1]{vaserstein1976foundations} gives the central-extension theorem and dates the field case to Steinberg's 1962 work; the modern general formulation is also treated in \citet[III, \S5]{weibel2013kbook}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established for perfect groups and for the stated stable linear group. The additional hermitian and simplicial claims are separated in the next item.

title: The incompletely specified higher hermitian simplicial model
notes: The page writes \(0\to K_2O(A)\to\operatorname{St}O(A)\to EO(A)\to0\), calls it a universal central extension, and proposes \(K_nO(A)=\pi_{n-1}O(A)\). A question asks which finite subsets should be simplices; triangular unipotent matrices and their left and right translates are sketched. The ordinary linear analogue appears in the margin.
statement: A precise higher hermitian construction must specify \((A,*,\varepsilon,\Lambda)\), the stable elementary unitary subgroup, its generators and root relations, the admissible triangular subgroups, and the simplicial realization whose homotopy groups are intended. The surviving sketches do not determine all these data or establish comparison with a particular modern Grothendieck--Witt spectrum. The notation \(\pi_{n-1}O(A)\) cannot mean homotopy of the discrete group alone.
reconstruction: The general perfect-group theorem is retained separately in 1971-246.12. The ordinary Volodin model explains the method, but importing its linear comparison theorem does not identify the complete hermitian theory suggested here.
fate: The prior stable form-group framework is \citet{vaserstein1970stabilization}; the linear simplicial method was published in \citet{volodin1971extraordinary}. Searches of Vaserstein's subsequent foundations papers found the ordinary associative-ring comparison \citep{vaserstein1973foundations,vaserstein1976foundations}, not a uniquely matching all-parameter hermitian statement for this sketch.
present_status: As of November 2026: the proposed model remains underdetermined by the notes. This classification concerns identification, not a claim that modern hermitian K-theory remains undeveloped.

title: Projective K0 and elementary-matrix K1
notes: The opening formulas are \(K_0(A)\) as the Grothendieck group of projective modules of finite rank and \(K_1(A)=GL(\infty,A)/E(A)\). A triangular sketch is followed by the explicit statement that \(E(A)\) is generated by all elementary matrices. A Helmholtz colour-subtraction analogy illustrates group completion.
statement: For a unital associative ring \(A\), \(K_0(A)\) is the group completion of isomorphism classes of finitely generated projective right modules under direct sum. Set \(GL(A)=\varinjlim GL_n(A)\) under \(g\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(g,1)\), and let \(E(A)\) be generated by \(1+ae_{ij}\), \(i\ne j\). Then \(E(A)=[GL(A),GL(A)]\), so \(K_1(A)\) is the abelianization. A single upper triangular subgroup is not \(E(A)\).
reconstruction: The later generator sentence governs the earlier schematic drawing. The colour analogy is treated as pedagogy, not as a claim of a mathematical identification with physical colour spaces.
fate: The exact stable definitions and commutator result occur in \citet[\S12]{bass1964stable} and \citet[Proposition 0]{basshellerswan1964whitehead}, well before the lecture.
present_status: As of November 2026: standard definitions, with finite generation and stabilization retained.

title: Steinberg relations and the incomplete displayed presentation
notes: Two displayed relations are additivity and \([E_{ij}(a),E_{jk}(b)]=E_{ik}(ab)\). The four-factor line above them has overwritten signs and right side \(1\). The abstract group with the relations is called \(St(A)\).
statement:
In the stable Steinberg group use generators \(x_{ij}(a)\), \(i
e j\), with \(x_{ij}(a)x_{ij}(b)=x_{ij}(a+b)\), \([x_{ij}(a),x_{kl}(b)]=1\) when \(j
e k\) and \(i
e l\), and \([x_{ij}(a),x_{jk}(b)]=x_{ik}(ab)\) for distinct \(i,j,k\), with a consistent commutator convention. The four factors with adjacent roots do not in general multiply to the identity: with inverse signs in the first pair they yield \(1+ab e_{ik}\).
reconstruction: The missing disjoint-root relation and distinct-index conditions are supplied. The overwritten first signs are left diplomatically unresolved; the erroneous identity right side is a separate mathematical defect.
fate: See \citet[\S6]{vaserstein1976foundations} for the explicit stable Steinberg presentation and its low-degree role. These relations and Milnor's \(K_2\) are antecedent theory, not Kazhdan's new theorem.
present_status: As of November 2026: the completed presentation is standard; the notes' two displayed relations alone do not specify it fully.

title: K2 as the central kernel of the stable Steinberg group
notes: The notes write \(K_2(A)=\ker(St(A)\to E(A))\) and describe it informally as relations other than the standard ones.
statement: For a unital associative ring, send \(x_{ij}(a)\) to \(1+ae_{ij}\). The stable Steinberg group is the universal central extension of the perfect group \(E(A)\), and \(K_2(A)\cong H_2(E(A),\mathbb Z)\). The kernel is a group of relation classes modulo Steinberg relations, not a free list of extra relators.
reconstruction: Centrality, universality, and the stable range are made explicit. No analogous universal-extension assertion is made for every finite-rank \(St_n(A)\).
fate: The low-degree theory was available before February 1972 in Milnor's introduction; the publisher dates its edition to January 1972. The precise extension theorem was read in \citet[Theorem 6.1]{vaserstein1976foundations}; see also \citet{milnor1972introduction} for historical publication metadata.
present_status: As of November 2026: established stable algebraic \(K_2\), independent of the later proposed higher models.

title: The determinant identifies K1 of a field
notes: The determinant-one subgroup of \(GL(4,\mathbb C)\) is said to be generated by elementary matrices. The final \(\mathbb C\) in \(K_1(\mathbb C)=\mathbb C\) has an uncertain upper mark, followed by ``and this holds for any field''.
statement: For a commutative field \(F\), elementary row operations give \(SL_n(F)=E_n(F)\) for \(n\ge2\), and determinant induces \(K_1(F)\cong F^\times\). For a division ring the replacement is the abelianization of its unit group, rather than an ordinary determinant into its underlying additive group.
reconstruction: The multiplicative group symbol is supplied mathematically; the scan does not justify claiming that the uncertain mark is definitely a legible star.
fate: This is the familiar field case of the stable Whitehead group; see \citet[Proposition 0 and the division-ring corollary after Theorem 1]{basshellerswan1964whitehead}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established. The additive group of \(F\) is not the target.

title: Are universally valid elementary relations consequences of the Steinberg relations?
notes: The page explicitly labels as unsolved the question whether a relation valid in every ring follows from the Steinberg relations. It also mentions an unidentified problem in discrete group theory as a trivial case.
statement: A precise augmented formulation is as follows. Let \(R=\mathbb Z\langle x_s:s\in S\rangle\) be the free associative unital ring, with augmentation \(\epsilon:R\to\mathbb Z\) sending every variable to zero. Then \(\ker(K_2(R)\xrightarrow{\epsilon_*}K_2(\mathbb Z))=0\). Consequently a stable word in elementary generators that is the identity as a universal matrix and whose Steinberg lift becomes the identity after augmentation is already a consequence of the Steinberg relations. In particular this applies when every entry has zero constant term. Allowing arbitrary constant relations without this normalization introduces the nonzero group \(K_2(\mathbb Z)\).
reconstruction: The augmentation condition is reconstructed from the subsequent use of free rings without identity. It expresses reduced \(K_2\)-vanishing without identifying the naive Steinberg kernel of an arbitrary nonunital ring with that reduced group. The cryptic discrete-group subproblem is not identifiable.
fate: Vaserstein announces the answer on P000413. \citet[second theorem, p.231]{vaserstein1973foundations} states free nonunital acyclicity; \citet[Theorem 28.1 and Corollary 28.1]{vaserstein1976foundations} gives precisely \(K_n(\mathbb Z)\cong K_n(\mathbb Z\langle S\rangle)\) and its reduced consequence, with Gersten's proof cited for higher degrees. The supplied earlier-year index contains no exact recurrence. The match is partial because the February wording does not spell out the augmentation convention.
present_status: As of November 2026: the augmented universal-relation statement is resolved. The literal unnormalized statement must be qualified; it is not a remaining open problem.

title: Embedding K0 as a Laurent K1 summand
notes: For \(B=A[t,t^{-1}]\), an automorphism of a finite projective module is embedded into an automorphism of a free module by adjoining the identity on a complement. Multiplication by \(t\) on \(P\otimes_A B\) defines \(K_0(A)\to K_1(B)\).
statement: For \(P\oplus Q\cong A^r\), take the class of \(t\,1_{P_B}\oplus1_{Q_B}\) in \(K_1(B)\). It is independent of the complement and free identification, additive in \(P\), and defines a split injection \(K_0(A)\hookrightarrow K_1(B)\). The indeterminate is central, also when \(A\) is noncommutative.
reconstruction: The projective-automorphism definition explains why the construction does not require \(P\) itself to be free.
fate: The construction is the map \(h\) of \citet[pp.62--63 and \S5]{basshellerswan1964whitehead}. Their regular-ring decomposition predates the talk; the summand construction and index remain meaningful more generally, with Nil terms retained.
present_status: As of November 2026: standard part of the fundamental theorem for Laurent polynomial \(K\)-theory.

title: Polynomial cokernels and the normalization of the Laurent index
notes: Write a Laurent invertible matrix \(L=t^{-n}L'\) with polynomial entries in \(L'\); its cokernel is said to be a finite projective \(A\)-module. The page calls this the inverse projection but does not subtract the shift contribution.
statement: If \(g\in GL_r(A[t,t^{-1}])\), choose \(n\ge0\) with \(t^ng\in M_r(A[t])\). The Laurent index is \(\partial[g]=[\operatorname{coker}(t^ng:A[t]^r\to A[t]^r)]-nr[A]\). The cokernel is finite projective as an \(A\)-module. Increasing \(n\) by one adds \(r[A]\) to the first term, so the difference is independent of \(n\), and \(\partial h[P]=[P]\).
reconstruction: The subtractive term is required; record 249 supplies it explicitly. The formula is written for stable classes, not claimed to turn two nonisomorphic polynomial cokernels into isomorphic modules.
fate: This is the index construction behind \citet[\S5]{basshellerswan1964whitehead}; the modern version is also given in \citet[III, \S3]{weibel2013kbook}. The following week's return to it is a clarification of an old construction.
present_status: As of November 2026: established after normalization. Using only the cokernel class would assign a nonzero answer to the identity when one chooses \(n>0\).

title: The K1 summand in Laurent K2
notes: Beside \(K_0(A)\subset K_1(B)\), the notes assert that \(K_1(A)\) is a direct summand of \(K_2(B)\), and leave construction of the forward map as an exercise.
statement: For a unital associative ring \(A\) and central \(t\), the Laurent fundamental theorem has a natural split summand \(K_1(A)\subset K_2(A[t,t^{-1}])\); in full generality \(K_2(B)\cong K_2(A)\oplus K_1(A)\oplus NK_2(A)\oplus NK_2(A)\), where \(NK_2(A)=\ker(K_2(A[t])\to K_2(A))\).
reconstruction: The full modern decomposition is supplied to prevent suppressing the two Nil terms. The notebook asserts only the indicated summand.
fate: \citet{gersten1971laurent} had already proved a related regular-ring surjectivity result (received June 1970, printed October 1971), not the exact general decomposition. The general statement is among the explicit Laurent formulas of \citet[third theorem, p.231]{vaserstein1973foundations}; record 253 returns to it and cites Wagoner in the notes. The class records the checked general publication rather than attributing priority solely to this lecture.
present_status: As of November 2026: established; omission of Nil terms is justified only under additional regularity or vanishing hypotheses.

title: Truncation modulo finite matrices as a boundary construction
notes: Two-sided row-and-column-finite matrices are truncated to one side. A marginal correction restricts them to finitely many diagonals parallel to the main diagonal. A lifted elementary relation has image \(1\) modulo finite matrices and is then described as a finite matrix representing \(K_1(A)\).
statement: For two-sided finite-band matrices, compression to the nonnegative half-line is multiplicative modulo the ideal of finitely supported matrices: the defect factors through only finitely many indices at the cut. Laurent multiplication matrices lie in this algebra. Lifting a Steinberg relation through the compression produces an invertible \(1+F\) with \(F\) finitely supported, hence a stable \(K_1(A)\)-class. It is \(L-1\), not \(L\), that has finite support.
reconstruction: This reconstructs the algebraic Toeplitz boundary and makes explicit the finite-support defect. Independence of lifts is part of the boundary theorem; the notebook's sketches alone are not a proof.
fate: The general suspension and exact-sequence treatment is published by \citet[first--third theorems]{vaserstein1973foundations}. Prior Laurent constructions appear in \citet{basshellerswan1964whitehead,gersten1971laurent}, but the retrieved earlier sources do not establish priority for this exact general Toeplitz implementation. Class B records the verified later formulation by another author, with the match qualified because the notebook provides only a sketch.
present_status: As of November 2026: standard after imposing the notebook's own bandwidth correction and reading the last matrix as identity plus a finite matrix.

title: An integral polarization and Hodge decomposition
notes: For a nonsingular complex projective \(X\) of dimension \(d\), the notes introduce \(H^n(X,\mathbb Z)\), its complexification, and a closed integral \((1,1)\)-form \(\eta\), called a polarization. They write \(H^n(X,\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}\).
statement: For smooth projective \(X/\mathbb C\), take \(\eta=c_1(L)\) for an ample line bundle, represented by a K\"ahler form. Then \(H^n(X,\mathbb C)=\bigoplus H^{p,q}(X)\), with \(\overline{H^{p,q}}=H^{q,p}\). The integral lattice for a pure integral Hodge structure is \(H^n(X,\mathbb Z)/\mathrm{torsion}\); complexification kills torsion.
reconstruction: An arbitrary integral closed \((1,1)\)-class need not be positive. Ampleness/K\"ahler positivity and the torsion-free lattice are the missing qualifications.
fate: These are the prerequisites of the already published survey \citet[\S2]{griffiths1970periods} and the pure-Hodge definitions of \citet[\S2.1]{deligne1971hodge}. Griffiths's text derives from a 1968 address and appeared in March 1970.
present_status: As of November 2026: established classical Hodge theory under the stated compactness and positivity hypotheses.

title: Hard Lefschetz, primitive cohomology, and orthogonal decomposition
notes: The operator \(\eta\) raises bidegree by \((1,1)\). Primitive cohomology is the kernel of a high power of \(\eta\), and the notes decompose cohomology into powers of \(\eta\) times primitive pieces.
statement: Let \(L=\eta\smile-\). For \(0\le n\le d\), \(L^{d-n}:H^n(X,\mathbb Q)\to H^{2d-n}(X,\mathbb Q)\) is an isomorphism. Put \(P^n=\ker(L^{d-n+1}:H^n\to H^{2d-n+2})\). Then \(H^n=\bigoplus_{j\ge0}L^jP^{n-2j}\), and this decomposition respects Hodge types. With a K\"ahler metric the associated primitive Lefschetz components are orthogonal for the Hodge inner product.
reconstruction: The degree range, coefficient field, and which inner product supplies orthogonality are stated explicitly; the formula for primitive degree is not extended beyond its intended range without reinterpretation.
fate: \citet[\S2, pp.234--235]{griffiths1970periods} explicitly passes to primitive cohomology and gives the Lefschetz decomposition; this is classical input to the variation theory.
present_status: As of November 2026: established, not an instance of the Hodge conjecture.

title: Hodge--Riemann bilinear relations and a sign inconsistency
notes: The notes use \(\Psi(x,y)=(-1)^{n(n+1)/2}\int_X\eta^{d-n}\wedge x\wedge y\). They state \(i^{p-q}\Psi(x,\bar x)>0\) and later require \(\Psi(x,C\bar x)>0\), where \(C|_{H^{p,q}}=i^{p-q}\).
statement: On primitive \(H^{p,q}\), \(p+q=n\le d\), let \(Q(x,y)=(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}\int_Xx\wedge y\wedge\eta^{d-n}\). Then \(Q(y,x)=(-1)^nQ(x,y)\), \(Q(H^{p,q},H^{r,s})=0\) unless \((r,s)=(q,p)\), and \(i^{p-q}Q(x,\bar x)>0\) for \(x\ne0\). With the notebook's \(\Psi=(-1)^nQ\), positivity is instead \(i^{q-p}\Psi(x,\bar x)>0\), equivalently \(\Psi(x,C\bar x)>0\).
reconstruction: Two consistent conventions are displayed rather than altering one sign without explanation. The source's first and last positivity assertions differ in odd weight.
fate: Compare the polarization conventions in \citet[\S2 and equations (9.8)--(9.9)]{griffiths1970periods} and \citet[Definition 2.1.16]{deligne1971hodge}. The scan confirms both the \(n(n+1)/2\) exponent and \(i^{p-q}\) in the first inequality.
present_status: As of November 2026: the bilinear relations are established; the literal combination of signs in the notes fails already in weight one.

title: Abstract polarized Hodge structures and the Weil operator
notes: The end replaces geometric cohomology by a finite-dimensional vector space with a real form, a \((p,q)\)-decomposition, the operator \(C\), and a bilinear form satisfying symmetry and positivity conditions.
statement: A real Hodge structure of weight \(n\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space \(V\) with \(V_\mathbb C=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}V^{p,q}\), \(\overline{V^{p,q}}=V^{q,p}\). A polarization additionally has the type orthogonality and signed positivity stated in the preceding item. The Weil operator is real on \(V\), acts by \(i^{p-q}\) on \(V^{p,q}\), and satisfies \(C^2=(-1)^n\). An integral structure adds a lattice; invariance under \(C\) alone does not replace full Hodge-type orthogonality.
reconstruction: The distinction between a real structure and an integral lattice is made explicit. This is a definition and does not assert that every abstract polarized Hodge structure comes from a smooth projective variety.
fate: See \citet[\S2.1, especially Definition 2.1.16]{deligne1971hodge} and \citet[\S9]{griffiths1970periods}. Both were published before Gabrielov's report.
present_status: As of November 2026: standard linear-algebraic structure used in variations and period domains.

title: The shift-independent Laurent index revisited
notes: Kirillov writes \(M=t^{-k}M_1=t^{-\ell}M_2\), observes that polynomial multiplication has zero kernel, and explicitly adds ``one must subtract the excess''. The same symbol \(k\) is also used for matrix size.
statement: For \(g\in GL_r(A[t,t^{-1}])\) and \(N\) large enough, define \(\partial[g]=[\operatorname{coker}(t^Ng)]-Nr[A]\). The first cokernel is finite projective over \(A\). Multiplying by another \(t\) changes its class by \(r[A]\), proving independence of \(N\). Elementary changes preserve the resulting stable index; arbitrary Laurent elementary changes need not preserve a chosen polynomial cokernel before normalization.
reconstruction: Separate symbols \(r,N\) prevent confusing size with denominator-clearing order. The positive-cokernel convention is chosen so that multiplication by \(t\) has index \(+[A]\); the analytic Fredholm convention would have the opposite sign.
fate: This clarifies occurrence 1971-247.7. The index construction was already in \citet[\S5]{basshellerswan1964whitehead}; see \citet[III, \S3]{weibel2013kbook} for the general form.
present_status: As of November 2026: established; the new lecture's significance is the recorded repair of the missing normalization.

title: The projective-module splitting and Gelfand’s repetition
notes: For \(N\oplus M=A^r\), the automorphism \(t\) on \(N_B\) and \(1\) on \(M_B\) gives a free \(B\)-matrix. The notes compute \(\operatorname{coker}(t:N[t]\to N[t])=N\). Gelfand repeats the diagram, whose displayed scalar-extended module is erroneously labelled \(A^r\).
statement: The matrix for \(t1_{N_B}\oplus1_{M_B}\) is already polynomial after choosing an \(A\)-linear free identification \(N\oplus M\cong A^r\). Its polynomial cokernel is \(N\), so \(\partial h=1\) on \(K_0(A)\). Scalar extension yields \(N_B\oplus M_B\cong B^r\), not \(A^r\).
reconstruction: This verifies one side of the splitting and does not assert that the two maps are inverses on all of \(K_1(B)\), which contains the other summands.
fate: The map and its left inverse are those of \citet[pp.62--63 and \S5]{basshellerswan1964whitehead}. The two recorded explanations are part of the same construction, not two separate discoveries.
present_status: As of November 2026: established; the module label requires correction.
speaker: A. A. Kirillov; intervention by I. M. Gelfand

title: The Laurent exact sequence and polynomial Nil summands
notes: The notes display \(0\to K_1(A)\to K_1(A[t])\oplus K_1(A[t^{-1}])\to K_1(A[t,t^{-1}])\to K_0(A)\to0\), and \(K_1(A[t])=K_1(A)\oplus\operatorname{Nil}A\). They say that Nil vanishes for regular rings.
statement: For a unital ring, set \(NK_1(A)=\ker(K_1(A[t])\xrightarrow{t\mapsto0}K_1(A))\). Evaluation splits the polynomial group. The displayed Laurent sequence, with opposite signs on the two constant inclusions, is exact and its right boundary is split by \(h\). Thus \(K_1(A[t,t^{-1}])\cong K_1(A)\oplus K_0(A)\oplus NK_1(A)^{\oplus2}\). If \(A\) is left regular noetherian (every finite left module has finite projective dimension), then \(NK_1(A)=0\).
reconstruction: The definition of regularity and the two copies of the Nil group are supplied. ``Functions on the suspension'' on P000405 is an index-theoretic analogy: algebraically the Laurent extension corresponds to product with the multiplicative group, not literally to a topological suspension.
fate: \citet[Theorems 1--2]{basshellerswan1964whitehead} prove the regular version; \citet[III, Theorem 3.6 and \S3]{weibel2013kbook} gives the general formulation including Nil groups. Earlier item 1968-171.8 concerns related polynomial matrices, but no identical indexed problem was located.
present_status: As of November 2026: established, with regularity essential for deleting Nil terms.

title: Higman linearization and nilpotent matrices
notes: After removing the constant \(K_1\)-part, the notes write \(M=1+tN(t)\). Enlarging the matrix reduces higher powers to first order, so \(N\) becomes constant, and polynomial invertibility forces \(N^k=0\).
statement: A polynomial matrix invertible over \(A[t]\) with constant term \(I\) becomes, after stabilization and elementary equivalence, \(I-tN\) for a finite nilpotent matrix \(N\) over \(A\). Conversely \(I-tN\) is polynomially invertible exactly when \(N\) is nilpotent, with inverse the finite geometric series. Nilpotent endomorphisms supply generators and relations for the Nil group; their raw set of matrices is not itself a group.
reconstruction: The sign of \(N\) is conventional. Stable equivalence, rather than equality of the original matrices, is the content of the linearization.
fate: This is the classical Higman trick, used in \citet[Proposition 2.1 and its proof]{basshellerswan1964whitehead} and explained in \citet[III, \S3]{weibel2013kbook}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established and still a useful computational model of polynomial Nil phenomena.

title: Killing a perfect normal subgroup by the plus construction
notes: For \(H\triangleleft\pi_1(X)\), \(H=[H,H]\), the notes attach two- and three-cells, obtain \(\pi_1(X_H)=\pi_1(X)/H\), and preserve integral homology. They claim uniqueness up to homotopy and functoriality.
statement: For a connected CW complex \(X\) and a perfect normal subgroup \(H\), there is a plus construction \(X\to X_H^+\) obtained by attaching cells in dimensions 2 and 3, with fundamental group quotient \(\pi_1(X)/H\). The map is acyclic: it induces homology isomorphisms with every local coefficient module over that quotient. The resulting map under \(X\) is unique up to homotopy. Ordinary untwisted homology alone is not the full characterization.
reconstruction: CW hypotheses, local coefficients, and uniqueness of the map under \(X\) are supplied. The phrase ``homology ring'' is replaced by homology groups unless an additional multiplication is given.
fate: Quillen's construction circulated before the lecture; \citet[IV, Theorem 1.5 and Lemma 1.6]{weibel2013kbook} dates the announcement to 1969 and gives the acyclic-map formulation. Vaserstein's 1973 announcement cites Quillen's 1970 ICM account as an existing definition.
present_status: As of November 2026: established. The local-coefficient condition is essential to the stated uniqueness formulation.

title: The discrete GL plus model and the missing degree zero
notes: Morava stresses that \(GL(R)\) is discrete, kills its perfect elementary subgroup, and defines \(K_i(R)=\pi_i(BGL(R)^+)\). The crossed-out line about \(K_0\) is replaced by a note that the definition must change because the space is connected.
statement: For a unital associative ring \(R\), define \(K_i(R)=\pi_i(BGL(R)^+)\) for \(i\ge1\), where plus kills the stable elementary subgroup. A representing space for connective algebraic \(K\)-theory is \(K_0(R)\times BGL(R)^+\), with the group of components \(K_0(R)\). Its fundamental group is \(GL(R)/E(R)\).
reconstruction: The subscript range and component factor are explicitly restored. The source itself notices the degree-zero issue, so this is not counted as an uncorrected false theorem.
fate: This is Quillen's plus definition as summarized in \citet[IV, \S1]{weibel2013kbook}; the comparison with the earlier low groups is included in \citet[first theorem]{vaserstein1973foundations}.
present_status: As of November 2026: standard connective algebraic \(K\)-theory; connectedness of \(BGL^+\) remains compatible with nonzero \(K_0\).

title: Agreement of Quillen K2 with the classical field group
notes: The notes attribute to Quillen the equality \(K_2^{\mathrm{Quillen}}(R)=k_2^{\mathrm{Milnor}}(R)\) for a field.
statement: For a field \(F\), Quillen's \(\pi_2BGL(F)^+\) agrees with the classical Steinberg-kernel \(K_2(F)\), and Matsumoto's theorem identifies it with \((F^\times\otimes_{\mathbb Z}F^\times)/\langle a\otimes(1-a):a\ne0,1\rangle\). Agreement with the stable Steinberg-kernel definition holds for unital rings as well; the symbolic presentation stated here is the field case.
reconstruction: The modern distinction between Milnor's original ring \(K_2\) and the Milnor symbol group of a field is made explicit; no assertion is extended to equality of higher Milnor and Quillen groups.
fate: The low-degree identification belongs to the original plus theory; see \citet[IV, \S1]{weibel2013kbook} and the explicit \(K_2\)-identification in \citet[first theorem]{vaserstein1973foundations}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established in degree two. The field qualification does not justify replacing all higher algebraic \(K\)-groups by Milnor symbols.

title: Discrete and topological general linear groups give different theories
notes: After insisting on discreteness, Morava says that a version for topological groups gives the usual \(K\)-functor for \(\mathbb R\) and \(\mathbb C\), and mentions Volodin's alternative definition.
statement: Using \(GL_n(\mathbb C)\) or \(GL_n(\mathbb R)\) with their analytic topologies and group completion leads to the representing spaces \(\mathbb Z\times BU\) and \(\mathbb Z\times BO\) for connective complex and real topological \(K\)-theory. Using the same fields as discrete rings yields algebraic \(K\)-theory. The continuous inclusion from the discrete group induces a comparison map, not an equality of the theories.
reconstruction: The precise spaces clarify the dependence on topology. Periodic topological \(K\)-theory additionally inverts Bott periodicity; it is not obtained by changing only the notation for \(K_0\).
fate: The distinction is built into the classical classifying-space approach and is reviewed alongside algebraic models in \citet[IV, \S1]{weibel2013kbook}. Volodin's original construction was published in 1971, received July 1970 \citep{volodin1971extraordinary}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established comparison of different functors; their values must not be substituted for one another.

title: Cohomology on spaces from the K-theory representing space
notes: A displayed definition reads \(K_i(R)(Y)=[S^i\wedge Y;X_{E(R)}]\), with a bracket labelled suspension.
statement: For a pointed CW complex \(Y\), stable algebraic \(K\)-cohomology is defined by the connective \(K(R)\)-spectrum. Its reduced groups satisfy \(\widetilde K(R)^{-i}(Y)=[\Sigma^iY,\Omega^\infty K(R)]_*\) for \(i\ge0\), with the appropriate base component when \(\Sigma^iY\) is connected. The full zeroth space includes \(K_0(R)\). An arbitrary pointed space without compatible deloopings does not by itself define a generalized cohomology theory in every degree.
reconstruction: Based homotopy classes, degree-sign convention, component information, and the spectrum structure are supplied. The page is a motivation for a cohomology theory, not a complete construction of its deloopings.
fate: Quillen already announces Segal's coherent categorical cohomology theory in \citet[\S3, p.50]{quillen1971cohomology}, reporting at Nice in 1970 and printed in 1971. The detailed construction appears in \citet[\S\S1--4]{segal1974categories}, received in August 1972. Thus the later publication date does not make the seminar's basic assertion a new post-lecture development.
present_status: As of November 2026: standard representability once the infinite-loop-space structure is included.

title: Novikov’s Chern-character programme
